title: The Book of Enoch: A Black Reader's Study Edition - Part 1
subtitle: Start Here: How to Use This Book, A Note on the Text, the Reader's Charter, and the Prologue
description:
Before any angel speaks in this book, before any judge takes a seat or any record is opened, there is a sound. It comes from below.

This is Start Here, the opening part of The Book of Enoch: A Black Reader’s Study Edition. It gathers everything that comes before Part One: how the book is built, which translation it prints and how, the Reader’s Charter, and the Prologue.

Inside this part

  • How to Use This Book — how to read it straight through and how to use it as a reference.
  • A Note on the Text — which translation the Reading Text is, and how this edition presents it.
  • The Reader’s Charter — the study’s commitments, set before the Prologue.
  • Prologue: The First Cry — states the claim of the whole study: First Enoch is a cry-and-judgment book from the underside of empire, and it survives whole because an African church kept it.

An honest edition

The Reading Text is R. H. Charles’s 1917 translation, made from the Ethiopic and in the public domain. It is not a new translation, and it has not yet been checked line by line against a Ge’ez manuscript; the book says so plainly. This first digital edition is a pre-publication manuscript, and the book’s release notes list reviews still required before print. It is an independent work of study, not an official publication of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and it does not speak for it.

Digital edition (PDF), 26 pages. Instant access from your Account page after purchase. This is part 1 of 5 of a 527-page volume (pages 7–26 of the complete book, plus cover and front matter). The complete volume is also sold separately as The Book of Enoch: A Black Reader’s Study Edition - Full Version.
what_you_learn: How the book is built, and how to read it straight through or look things up
Which translation the Reading Text is, and what this edition changed in it
The four parts of the study's claim: Kept, Kin in reading, Addressed and Carried
The four movements the book keeps returning to: it cries, it records, it reverses, and it is carried
Why the Prologue begins with a sound: the earth's accusation (7:6) and a cry that went up to heaven (8:4)
who_for:
• Bible readers who have heard of Enoch and want to read the book itself, not just quotations from it.
  • Black Christians and readers of African heritage who want to read the book an African church kept, in conversation with their own tradition.
  • Pastors, teachers and small-group leaders.
  • Curious readers who want a sourced, calm alternative to sensational claims about “the forbidden book.”
  • Readers who want to see how the study argues before they buy the longer parts.

No background in Ge’ez, Hebrew or Greek is needed. No one is asked to change churches or canons.

What am I holding, and who kept it for me? Where does harm come from, and what does heaven do first?

title: The Book of Enoch: A Black Reader's Study Edition - Part 4
subtitle: Booklet 3 of 3: The Dream Visions, the Epistle, and Reading After the Last Page (1 Enoch 83-108)
description:
How does a people tell its own history when it is under pressure? What does a dying teacher hand on?

This part holds Parts Five, Six and Seven of the study (Chapters 18–31, with 1 Enoch 83–108). It is the longest of the three booklets. It reads the Dream Visions, the Epistle of Enoch, and then steps back from the last page to ask what the book leaves in our hands.

Inside this part

  • Part Five: The Dream Visions — a short, terrifying dream in which heaven falls, and a long one that retells history from Adam with every person drawn as an animal. Chapters 18-22.
  • Part Six: The Epistle of Enoch — a father’s final words, with its ten weeks, its woes and its hope, then the birth of Noah and a last chapter that survives only in Ge’ez. Chapters 23-26.
  • Part Seven: Reading Enoch After the Last Page — “The Church That Kept Enoch,” “Africa in the Book, and the Book in Africa,” “Reading From Below,” “Five Things to Carry” and “What Enoch Leaves Us.”
  • The Reading Text — 1 Enoch 83-108 in R. H. Charles’s translation, set passage by passage beside the commentary.

A note on care

Two chapters in Part Five ask for particular care: Chapter 19 reads the colors of the animals and the ways those colors have been read, and Chapter 21 reads a vision in which the sheep are given a sword. The book invites you to take them at your own pace.

It is not a new translation, and it has not yet been checked line by line against a Ge’ez manuscript; the book says so plainly. This first digital edition is a pre-publication manuscript, and the book’s release notes list reviews still required before print. It is an independent work of study, not an official publication of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and it does not speak for it.

title: The Book of Enoch: A Black Reader's Study Edition - Part 5
subtitle: Back Matter: Appendices, Glossary, Bibliography, and Index
description:
The reference shelf of the study: an atlas of the book, a timeline, a ledger of every claim and a guide to the sources.

This part holds everything that comes after the last chapter of The Book of Enoch: A Black Reader’s Study Edition. It is a reference booklet: its entries point back to chapters and pages in the other parts, so it is most useful beside the main text.

Inside this part

  • Appendix A: An Atlas of the Book — the sections of 1 Enoch, their approximate dates, the ancient witnesses that preserve them and the threads that run across the whole book.
  • Appendix B: Where the English Leaves the Ge’ez — an honest appendix on the limits of the Reading Text.
  • Appendix C: A Timeline — from the book’s beginnings to the present.
  • Appendix D: The Foundation Ledger — what each kind of claim rests on and how far it has been checked.
  • Appendix E: A Source Guide — where to find the witnesses and the modern editions.
  • Glossary, Bibliography and Index — terms, sources and a page-number index for the complete volume.

An honest edition

The Reading Text is R. H. Charles’s 1917 translation, made from the Ethiopic and in the public domain. It is not a new translation, and it has not yet been checked line by line against a Ge’ez manuscript; the book says so plainly. This first digital edition is a pre-publication manuscript, and the book’s release notes list reviews still required before print. It is an independent work of study, not an official publication of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and it does not speak for it.
